claim: EB1 is a key cellular protein that delivers regulatory molecules throughout the cell via tip-tracking of growing microtubule plus-ends.
source: EB1 is a key cellular protein that delivers regulatory molecules throughout the cell via the tip-tracking of growing microtubule plus-ends.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that establishes the biological role of EB1.

claim: EB1 binds with higher affinity to GTP-tubulin subunits at the growing microtubule tip relative to GDP-tubulin along the microtubule length.
source: It is widely accepted that EB1 binds with higher affinity to GTP-tubulin subunits at the growing microtubule tip, relative to GDP-tubulin along the microtubule length.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing this differential affinity.

claim: EB1 binds to exposed microtubule protofilament-edge sites at a ~70 fold faster rate than to closed-lattice sites due to diffusional steric hindrance to binding.
source: Previously, we found that EB1 binds to exposed microtubule protofilament-edge sites at a ~70 fold faster rate than to closed-lattice sites, due to diffusional steric hindrance to binding.
evidence: This claim references previous experimental findings from the authors' prior work.

claim: A computational simulation with differential EB1 on-rates based on closed-lattice or protofilament-edge binding, and with EB1 off-rates dependent on tubulin hydrolysis state, robustly recapitulated experimental EB1 tip tracking.
source: A computational simulation with differential EB1 on-rates based on closed-lattice or protofilament-edge binding, and with EB1 off-rates that were dependent on the tubulin hydrolysis state, robustly recapitulated experimental EB1 tip tracking.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: DARPin binds exclusively to protofilament-edge sites and its binding site partially overlaps with the EB1 binding site.
source: we used cell-free biophysical assays, as well as live-cell imaging, in combination with a Designed Ankyrin Repeat Protein (DARPin) that binds exclusively to protofilament-edge sites, and whose binding site partially overlaps with the EB1 binding site.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pecqueur et al., 2012.

claim: DARPin blocked EB1 protofilament-edge binding, which led to a decrease in EB1 tip tracking on dynamic microtubules.
source: We found that DARPin blocked EB1 protofilament-edge binding, which led to a decrease in EB1 tip tracking on dynamic microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell-free and live-cell imaging experiments.

claim: Rapid EB1 binding to microtubule protofilament-edge sites contributes to robust EB1 tip tracking at the growing microtubule plus-end.
source: We conclude that rapid EB1 binding to microtubule protofilament-edge sites contributes to robust EB1 tip tracking at the growing microtubule plus-end.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by both simulation and experimental data.

claim: Microtubules are comprised of αβ tubulin heterodimers that are stacked end-to-end to form protofilaments, which associate laterally to form the hollow-tube structure of the microtubule.
source: Microtubules are important cellular filaments that are comprised of αβ tubulin heterodimers. The tubulin heterodimers are stacked end-to-end to form structures known as protofilaments, which associate laterally to form the hollow-tube structure of the microtubule (Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge about microtubule structure, supported by citation.

claim: The α/β polarity of the tubulin dimer induces microtubule polarity, such that the microtubule end with β-tubulin exposed forms the fast-growing, dynamic 'plus-end' of the microtubule.
source: The α/β polarity of the tubulin dimer induces microtubule polarity, such that the microtubule end with β-tubulin exposed forms the fast-growing, dynamic 'plus-end' of the microtubule (Desai and Mitchison, 1997; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge about microtubule polarity, supported by citations.

claim: The β-tubulin subunit binds to a GTP nucleotide in solution, which then hydrolyzes to GDP after incorporation into the microtubule lattice.
source: In solution, the β-tubulin subunit binds to a GTP nucleotide, which then hydrolyzes to GDP after incorporation into the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tubulin nucleotide binding and hydrolysis.

claim: Delayed GTP hydrolysis leads to a high concentration of GTP tubulin at the growing microtubule plus-end, commonly referred to as the 'GTP-cap'.
source: This delayed hydrolysis leads to a high concentration of GTP tubulin at the growing microtubule plus-end, commonly referred to as the 'GTP-cap' (Desai and Mitchison, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GTP-cap, supported by citation.

claim: The presence of the GTP-cap creates a distinct region that is present exclusively at growing microtubule ends.
source: The presence of the GTP-cap creates a distinct region that is present exclusively at growing microtubule ends (Maurer et al., 2011; Maurer et al., 2014; Zanic et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EB1 autonomously localizes to the growing ends of microtubules ('tip tracks') and recruits other important proteins that have little or no affinity to growing microtubule ends.
source: EB1 is a key cellular protein that autonomously localizes to the growing ends of microtubules ('tip tracks') and recruits other important proteins that have little or no affinity to growing microtubule ends (Bieling et al., 2007; Dixit et al., 2009; Morrison et al., 1998; Mustyatsa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Improper localization of EB1 at growing microtubule plus-ends can lead to disruptions in both cell division and cell migration.
source: It has been shown that improper localization of EB1 at growing microtubule plus-ends can lead to disruptions in both cell division and cell migration (Dema et al., 2023; Dong et al., 2010; Honoré et al., 2008; Mustyatsa et al., 2017; Rogers et al., 2002; van Haren et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: EB1 binds a small pocket within the microtubule lattice that is created by four tubulin dimers.
source: EB1 binds a small pocket within the microtubule lattice that is created by four tubulin dimers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EB1 binding site structure.

claim: EB1 binds with a higher affinity to GTP-tubulin subunits as compared to GDP-tubulin subunits.
source: It has been shown that EB1 binds with a higher affinity to GTP-tubulin subunits as compared to GDP-tubulin subunits. (Maurer et al., 2011; Maurer et al., 2012; Maurer et al., 2014; Zanic et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The difference in EB1 affinity for GTP versus GDP tubulin likely increases the enrichment of EB1 within the GTP-cap at growing microtubule plus-ends.
source: This difference in affinity likely increases the enrichment of EB1 within the GTP-cap at growing microtubule plus-ends.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential affinity of EB1 for GTP vs GDP tubulin.

claim: EB1 can bind to a partial binding pocket composed of 2–3 tubulin subunits, either at the tip of a protofilament, along the side of an exposed protofilament, or at lattice openings within the microtubule.
source: Recent work has demonstrated that EB1 can bind to a partial binding pocket composed of 2–3 tubulin subunits, either at the tip of a protofilament, along the side of an exposed protofilament, or at lattice openings within the microtubule (Reid et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: A partial EB1 binding site on the microtubule lattice led to a dramatic reduction in the diffusional steric hindrance that EB1 encounters in order to become properly oriented and then to slide into a closed, 4-tubulin binding pocket.
source: Here, a partial EB1 binding site on the microtubule lattice led to a dramatic reduction in the diffusional steric hindrance that EB1 encounters in order to become properly oriented and then to slide into a closed, 4-tubulin binding pocket.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism behind the faster on-rate at protofilament-edge sites.

claim: The expanded physical access afforded by EB1 binding to a partial, 2-tubulin binding pocket led to a ~70 fold increase in the EB1 on-rate compared to a closed 4-tubulin binding pocket.
source: In other words, the expanded physical access that is afforded by EB1 binding to a partial, 2-tubulin binding pocket (as compared to a closed 4-tubulin binding pocket) led to a ~70 fold increase in the EB1 on-rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous experimental data.

claim: Protofilament-edge sites are present at growing microtubule plus-ends.
source: Because protofilament-edge sites are present at growing microtubule plus-ends (Atherton et al., 2018; Gudimchuk et al., 2020; Guesdon et al., 2016), we hypothesized that this large difference in EB1 arrival rates could have important repercussions for the efficiency of EB1 tip tracking at growing microtubule plus-ends.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The rapid binding of EB1 to protofilament-edge sites at the growing microtubule plus-end could increase the efficiency of EB1 plus-end tip tracking.
source: We thus predicted that the rapid binding of EB1 to protofilament-edge sites at the growing microtubule plus-end could increase the efficiency of EB1 plus-end tip tracking.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the authors' hypothesis.

claim: The simulation incorporated the assembly and hydrolysis of individual tubulin subunits, as well as the binding and unbinding of EB1 molecules.
source: In this work, we generated a single-molecule stochastic simulation that incorporated the assembly and hydrolysis of individual tubulin subunits, as well as the binding and unbinding of EB1 molecules.
evidence: This describes the components of the computational model.

claim: In the simulation, EB1 bound rapidly to protofilament-edge sites and bound more slowly to closed-lattice sites.
source: Importantly, in our simulation, EB1 bound rapidly to protofilament-edge sites, and bound more slowly to closed-lattice sites.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the simulation model.

claim: The off-rate of EB1 from GTP-tubulin sites was low, with higher EB1 off-rates from GDP-tubulin sites.
source: In addition, consistent with previous affinity measurements, the off-rate of EB1 from GTP-tubulin sites was low, with higher EB1 off-rates from GDP-tubulin sites.
evidence: This describes another key feature of the simulation model, consistent with previous measurements.

claim: The simulation predicted that rapid binding to protofilament-edge sites increased the efficiency of EB1 tip-tracking at growing microtubule plus-ends.
source: The simulation predicted that rapid binding to protofilament-edge sites increased the efficiency of EB1 tip-tracking at growing microtubule plus-ends.
evidence: This is a prediction from the simulation results.

claim: DARPin suppressed EB1 protofilament-edge binding on stabilized microtubules.
source: We found that DARPin suppressed EB1 protofilament-edge binding on stabilized microtubules, and led to a disruption of EB1 tip tracking on dynamic microtubules plus-ends, both in cell-free experiments and in cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell-free assays.

claim: DARPin led to a disruption of EB1 tip tracking on dynamic microtubule plus-ends, both in cell-free experiments and in cells.
source: We found that DARPin suppressed EB1 protofilament-edge binding on stabilized microtubules, and led to a disruption of EB1 tip tracking on dynamic microtubules plus-ends, both in cell-free experiments and in cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both cell-free and live-cell experiments.

claim: Protofilament-edge binding, along with a differential EB1 binding affinity for GTP vs GDP tubulin, facilitates efficient EB1 tip tracking.
source: Together, our work predicts that protofilament-edge binding, along with a differential EB1 binding affinity for GTP vs GDP tubulin, facilitates efficient EB1 tip tracking.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by both simulation and experimental data.

claim: The microtubule assembly portion of the simulation utilized a previously published model in which individual tubulin subunits were allowed to arrive and depart from the growing microtubule plus-end.
source: The microtubule assembly portion of the simulation utilized a previously published model, in which individual tubulin subunits were allowed to arrive and depart from the growing microtubule plus-end (Margolin et al., 2011; Margolin et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the basis of the microtubule assembly component of the simulation.

claim: Once a tubulin subunit arrived at the growing microtubule plus-end, a longitudinal bond was immediately formed with its penultimate tubulin dimer.
source: Once a tubulin subunit arrived at the growing microtubule plus-end, a longitudinal bond was immediately formed with its penultimate tubulin dimer.
evidence: This describes a rule in the simulation model.

claim: Lateral bonds were stochastically formed in subsequent time steps after tubulin subunit arrival.
source: Then, lateral bonds were stochastically formed in subsequent time steps (Margolin et al., 2011; Margolin et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes a rule in the simulation model.

claim: Lattice-incorporated GTP-tubulin subunits were stochastically hydrolyzed to GDP-tubulin.
source: Finally, lattice-incorporated GTP-tubulin subunits were stochastically hydrolyzed to GDP-tubulin.
evidence: This describes a rule in the simulation model.

claim: The on-rate of new tubulin subunits to the microtubule plus-end depended on the simulated tubulin concentration.
source: In general, the on-rate of new tubulin subunits to the microtubule plus-end depended on the simulated tubulin concentration, and the off-rate of an individual tubulin subunit from the plus-end depended on its hydrolysis state and bonding state, where a GTP-tubulin subunit with two lateral bonds had the lowest off-rate in the simulation.
evidence: This describes rules in the simulation model.

claim: A GTP-tubulin subunit with two lateral bonds had the lowest off-rate in the simulation.
source: In general, the on-rate of new tubulin subunits to the microtubule plus-end depended on the simulated tubulin concentration, and the off-rate of an individual tubulin subunit from the plus-end depended on its hydrolysis state and bonding state, where a GTP-tubulin subunit with two lateral bonds had the lowest off-rate in the simulation.
evidence: This describes a rule in the simulation model.

claim: All parameter values for the microtubule assembly simulation matched a previously published parameter set, with the exception of the tubulin on-rate constant and one additional rule.
source: All of the parameter values for the microtubule assembly simulation matched a previously published parameter set (Margolin et al., 2012; Supplementary file 1), with the exception of (1) the tubulin on-rate constant, which was lowered in order to match our (slow) experimental growth rates, and (2) one additional rule was added to ensure that the tip taper at the microtubule plus-end matched our experimental values (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This describes the parameterization of the simulation model.

claim: The tubulin on-rate constant was lowered in order to match experimental growth rates.
source: All of the parameter values for the microtubule assembly simulation matched a previously published parameter set (Margolin et al., 2012; Supplementary file 1), with the exception of (1) the tubulin on-rate constant, which was lowered in order to match our (slow) experimental growth rates, and (2) one additional rule was added to ensure that the tip taper at the microtubule plus-end matched our experimental values (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This describes a modification to the simulation model to match experimental data.

claim: An additional rule was added to ensure that the tip taper at the microtubule plus-end matched experimental values.
source: All of the parameter values for the microtubule assembly simulation matched a previously published parameter set (Margolin et al., 2012; Supplementary file 1), with the exception of (1) the tubulin on-rate constant, which was lowered in order to match our (slow) experimental growth rates, and (2) one additional rule was added to ensure that the tip taper at the microtubule plus-end matched our experimental values (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This describes a modification to the simulation model to match experimental data.

claim: If the difference between the longest and the penultimate shortest protofilament exceeded 600 nm (75 dimers), the tubulin subunit off-rate and the lateral bond breakage rate were dramatically increased, quickly leading to a catastrophe event.
source: Here, if the difference between the longest and the penultimate shortest protofilament exceeded 600 nm (75 dimers), the tubulin subunit off-rate and the lateral bond breakage rate were dramatically increased, quickly leading to a catastrophe event.
evidence: This describes the additional rule added to the simulation model.

claim: Individual EB1 molecules were allowed to bind and unbind from their binding pockets at any position on the growing microtubule.
source: In addition to tubulin assembly, individual EB1 molecules were allowed to bind and unbind from their binding pockets at any position on the growing microtubule (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes a feature of the simulation model, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The EB1 on-rates and off-rates depended on the individual binding pocket chemistry and configuration.
source: However, the EB1 on-rates and off-rates depended on the individual binding pocket chemistry and configuration.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the EB1 binding model in the simulation.

claim: The on-rates for individual EB1 molecules depended on the structure of the binding pocket, such that EB1 arrivals to protofilament-edge sites were substantially faster than to closed-lattice sites, regardless of the hydrolysis state.
source: Specifically, the on-rates for individual EB1 molecules depended on the structure of the binding pocket, such that EB1 arrivals to protofilament-edge sites were substantially faster than to closed-lattice sites, regardless of the hydrolysis state (Figure 1A, top, see Methods) (Reid et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the EB1 binding model in the simulation, with reference to Figure 1A and previous work.

claim: The off-rate of EB1 molecules depended on the hydrolysis state of the EB1 binding site.
source: In contrast, the off-rate of EB1 molecules depended on the hydrolysis state of the EB1 binding site.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the EB1 binding model in the simulation.

claim: The tubulin subunits towards the minus end of the microtubule dictated the 'hydrolysis state' of the EB1 binding site.
source: Here, the tubulin subunits towards the minus end of the microtubule dictated the 'hydrolysis state' of the EB1 binding site.
evidence: This describes a rule in the simulation model.

claim: If 1–2 of the tubulin subunits towards the minus end were hydrolyzed to GDP, the binding site was considered to be a 'GDP' binding site, leading to an increased EB1 off-rate.
source: If 1–2 of these tubulin subunits were hydrolyzed to GDP, the binding site was considered to be a 'GDP' binding site, leading to an increased EB1 off-rate (Figure 1A, bottom, see Methods).
evidence: This describes a rule in the simulation model, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: All parameter values in the EB1 model were constrained by previously published experimental values, with the exception of the EB1 off-rate from protofilament-edge sites.
source: All parameter values in the EB1 model were constrained by previously published experimental values (Maurer et al., 2011; Maurer et al., 2014; Reid et al., 2019), with the exception of the EB1 off-rate from protofilament-edge sites, which has not been experimentally measured, but was constrained using bond energy arguments (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the parameterization of the EB1 binding model in the simulation.

claim: The EB1 off-rate from protofilament-edge sites has not been experimentally measured, but was constrained using bond energy arguments.
source: All parameter values in the EB1 model were constrained by previously published experimental values (Maurer et al., 2011; Maurer et al., 2014; Reid et al., 2019), with the exception of the EB1 off-rate from protofilament-edge sites, which has not been experimentally measured, but was constrained using bond energy arguments (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes how an unmeasured parameter was estimated in the simulation.

claim: Simulated EB1 behaved similarly to experiments, strongly targeting growing microtubule plus-ends while detaching from shortening ends.
source: Qualitatively, our simulated EB1 behaved similarly to experiments – strongly targeting growing microtubule plus-ends, while detaching from shortening ends (Figure 1B; Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental observations, with reference to Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: At a microtubule growth rate of 10–30 nm/s, the peak EB1 position has been reported to be ~144 nm distal of the microtubule tip.
source: At a microtubule growth rate of 10–30 nm/s, the peak EB1 position has been reported to be ~144 nm distal of the microtubule tip (Figure 1C, left, orange) (Roth et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The simulation produced a peak EB1 position of ~128 nm distal of the microtubule tip, similar to experimental observations.
source: We found that the simulation produced a peak EB1 position of ~128 nm distal of the microtubule tip, similar to experimental observations (Figure 1C, right, blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The growth rate and time to catastrophe for the simulated microtubules were similar to experimentally reported values.
source: We note that the growth rate and time to catastrophe for the simulated microtubules were similar to experimentally reported values (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E), and so the simulated peak EB1 position likely reflects an appropriately sized GTP-cap.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental data, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: The model with EB1 protofilament-edge binding reproduced the peak EB1 position without requiring a predetermined EB1 'exclusion zone'.
source: Importantly, our model with EB1 protofilament-edge binding reproduced the peak EB1 position without requiring a predetermined EB1 'exclusion zone,' as has been previously hypothesized (Maurer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and contrasts with a previous model.

claim: EB1 tip tracking in the model depended solely on EB1 on/off rates and a growing microtubule plus-end.
source: Rather, EB1 tip tracking in our current model depended solely on EB1 on/off rates and a growing microtubule plus-end.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the simulation model.

claim: The average tip standard deviation of simulated microtubules was 191±6 nm (mean ± SEM), similar to experimental measurements of 180 ± 17 nm.
source: We found that the average tip standard deviation of our simulated microtubules was 191±6 nm (mean ± SEM), similar to our experimental measurements of 180 ± 17 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B; Video 2, mean ± SEM).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental measurements, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B and Video 2.

claim: A slower GTP-tubulin hydrolysis rate increases EB1 binding along the microtubule, likely due to an increased concentration of GTP-tubulin within the microtubule lattice.
source: It has been shown that a slower GTP-tubulin hydrolysis rate increases EB1 binding along the microtubule, likely due to an increased concentration of GTP-tubulin within the microtubule lattice (Roostalu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A slower hydrolysis rate (0.05 s–1) led to an increased concentration of EB1 on the microtubule, as compared to the baseline simulation (0.55 s–1).
source: We found that a slower hydrolysis rate (0.05 s–1) led to an increased concentration of EB1 on the microtubule, as compared to the baseline simulation (0.55 s –1) (Figure 1D, Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 1D and Video 3.

claim: A slower hydrolysis rate led to a ~twofold increase in EB1 binding along the lattice of simulated microtubules relative to the baseline simulation, similar to previously reported experimental results.
source: By quantifying the localization of EB1 at growing microtubule plus-ends in these simulations, we observed a ~twofold increase in EB1 binding along the lattice of simulated microtubules with a slower hydrolysis rate, relative to the baseline simulation (Figure 1E, right, blue; calculated at position 768 nm, gray dashed line), similar to previously reported experimental results (Figure 1E, left, orange; Roostalu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results compared to experimental data, with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: EB1 tip tracking in the simulation depends on the tubulin hydrolysis rate, similar to previous experimental results.
source: This result demonstrates that EB1 tip tracking in the simulation depends on the tubulin hydrolysis rate, similar to previous experimental results (Roostalu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results compared to experimental data.

claim: EB1 monomers tip track less effectively than their dimer counterparts.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that EB1 monomers tip track less effectively than their dimer counterparts (Komarova et al., 2009; Skube et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The EB1 monomer off-rate was ~fourfold larger than the off-rates for dimers.
source: To determine how the model results would be impacted by including monomers in the model, rather than dimers, we turned to previous work, which demonstrated that the EB1 monomer off-rate was ~fourfold larger than the off-rates for dimers (Song et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EB1 tip tracking was decreased by ~threefold in the monomer simulations, consistent with previous reports.
source: We found that EB1 tip tracking was decreased by ~threefold in the monomer simulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), consistent with previous reports (Komarova et al., 2009; Skube et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results compared to previous experimental reports, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: An increased microtubule growth rate leads to a longer EB1 'comet'.
source: Finally, it has been widely reported that an increased microtubule growth rate leads to a longer EB1 'comet' (Farmer et al., 2021; Maurer et al., 2014; Reid et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: As the microtubule growth rate was increased in the simulation, the comet length was increased, similar to experimental reports.
source: Similar to experimental reports, we found that, as the microtubule growth rate was increased in the simulation, the comet length was increased (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results compared to experimental reports, with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: A higher EB1 closed-lattice on-rate led to EB1 accumulation at the growing microtubule end, but also led to EB1 accumulation along the length of the microtubule.
source: We found that, while a higher EB1 closed-lattice on-rate led to EB1 accumulation at the growing microtubule end, it also led to EB1 accumulation along the length of the microtubule (Figure 2A, right), thus reducing the specificity of EB1 localization to the growing microtubule end.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Increasing the EB1 closed-lattice on-rate reduced the specificity of EB1 localization to the growing microtubule end.
source: We found that, while a higher EB1 closed-lattice on-rate led to EB1 accumulation at the growing microtubule end, it also led to EB1 accumulation along the length of the microtubule (Figure 2A, right), thus reducing the specificity of EB1 localization to the growing microtubule end.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: An increasingly intense EB1-GFP puncta appeared at the growing microtubule end as the protofilament-edge on-rate was increased.
source: We found that an increasingly intense EB1-GFP puncta appeared at the growing microtubule end as the protofilament-edge on-rate was increased (Figure 2B, right; Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2B and Video 5.

claim: A low EB1 closed-lattice on-rate led to a clear EB1 puncta at the tip of the microtubule, where EB1 accumulation is dominated by protofilament-edge binding.
source: We found that a low EB1 closed-lattice on-rate led to a clear EB1 puncta at the tip of the microtubule (Figure 2C, left-bottom). Here, EB1 accumulation is dominated by protofilament-edge binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Increasing the EB1 closed-lattice on-rate by 32-fold led to a ~1.6 fold increase in EB1 intensity at the microtubule tip, but also led to a ~25 fold increase in EB1 intensity along the length of the microtubule.
source: However, increasing the EB1 closed-lattice on-rate by 32-fold led to a ~1.6 fold increase in EB1 intensity at the microtubule tip, but, importantly, also led to a ~25 fold increase in EB1 intensity along the length of the microtubule (Figure 2C, center), even in the presence of EB1 protofilament-edge binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: With increasing EB1 closed-lattice on-rates, the EB1 intensity at the microtubule tip was decreased relative to the lattice.
source: By plotting the ratio of Tip:Lattice EB1 intensity (see Methods), we found that, with increasing EB1 closed-lattice on-rates, the EB1 intensity at the microtubule tip was decreased relative to the lattice (Figure 2C, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The efficiency of simulated EB1 tip tracking was reduced with faster EB1 binding to closed-lattice sites, due to increased EB1 accumulation along the length of the microtubule.
source: Thus, the efficiency of simulated EB1 tip tracking was reduced with faster EB1 binding to closed-lattice sites, due to increased EB1 accumulation along the length of the microtubule.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: EB1 tip tracking was similar whether closed-lattice binding was on or off during the dynamic microtubule simulation.
source: We found that EB1 tip tracking was similar whether closed-lattice binding was on or off during the dynamic microtubule simulation (Figure 2D, cyan; Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2D and Video 6.

claim: By decreasing the protofilament-edge on-rate, the intensity of EB1 at the growing microtubule tip was dimmed.
source: We found that, by decreasing the protofilament-edge on-rate, the intensity of EB1 at the growing microtubule tip was dimmed (Figure 2E, left-bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: Upon increasing the protofilament-edge on-rate, the intensity of EB1 at the growing tip was increased, without an increase in EB1 intensity along the length of the microtubule.
source: Upon increasing the protofilament-edge on-rate, the intensity of EB1 at the growing tip was increased, without an increase in EB1 intensity along the length of the microtubule (Figure 2E, left-top).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: A 32-fold increase in the protofilament-edge on-rate led to a ~2.2 fold increase in EB1 intensity at the tip of the microtubule, and no change in the EB1 intensity along the length of the microtubule.
source: Here, a 32-fold increase in the protofilament-edge on-rate led to a ~2.2 fold increase in EB1 intensity at the tip of the microtubule, and, importantly, no change in the EB1 intensity along the length of the microtubule (Figure 2E, center).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: With increasing EB1 protofilament-edge on-rates, the EB1 intensity at the microtubule tip was increased relative to the lattice.
source: By plotting the ratio of Tip:Lattice EB1 intensity (see Methods), we found that, with increasing EB1 protofilament-edge on-rates, the EB1 intensity at the microtubule tip was increased relative to the lattice (Figure 2E, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: The efficiency of simulated EB1 tip tracking was enhanced by higher EB1 on-rates to incomplete, protofilament-edge binding sites.
source: Thus, the efficiency of simulated EB1 tip tracking was enhanced by higher EB1 on-rates to incomplete, protofilament-edge binding sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: EB1 tip tracking was rapidly diminished when protofilament-edge binding was shut off during a dynamic microtubule simulation, and returned quickly when the EB1 protofilament-edge on-rate was reset to its baseline value.
source: We found that EB1 tip tracking was rapidly diminished when protofilament-edge binding was shut off during a dynamic microtubule simulation, and returned quickly when the EB1 protofilament-edge on-rate was reset to its baseline value (Figure 2F, magenta; Video 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2F and Video 7.

claim: Distinct tip tracking was observed using the experimentally measured on-rate ratio for protofilament-edge sites relative to closed-lattice sites (50-100:1).
source: Importantly, distinct tip tracking was observed using the experimentally measured on-rate ratio for protofilament-edge sites relative to closed-lattice sites (50-100:1, Reid et al., 2019; Figure 2G, image B, gray dashed boxes).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results using experimentally measured parameters, with reference to Figure 2G.

claim: Clear tip tracking was observed using the experimentally measured off-rate ratio for GDP-tubulin relative to GTP-tubulin (calculated as 6–12).
source: Similar to the on-rate ratio, clear tip tracking was observed using the experimentally measured off-rate ratio for GDP-tubulin relative to GTP-tubulin (calculated as 6–12, based on KD values reported in Maurer et al., 2011; Figure 2H, image B, gray dashed boxes).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results using experimentally measured parameters, with reference to Figure 2H.

claim: In the absence of protofilament-edge binding, the experimentally observed range of closed-lattice GDP:GTP off-rate ratios did not reproduce EB1 tip tracking.
source: We found that, in the absence of protofilament-edge binding, the experimentally observed range of closed-lattice GDP:GTP off-rate ratios did not reproduce EB1 tip tracking (Figure 2I, top: representative simulated images; bottom: blue bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2I.

claim: By including a 50:1 protofilament-edge to closed-lattice on-rate ratio in the simulation, robust tip tracking was reproduced, with an increase in EB1 tip localization for a higher ratio of GDP:GTP off-rates.
source: However, by including a 50:1 protofilament-edge to closed-lattice on-rate ratio in the simulation, robust tip tracking was reproduced, with an increase in EB1 tip localization for a higher ratio of GDP:GTP off-rates (Figure 2I, red).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 2I.

claim: Based on the experimentally measured EB1 on and off rates, both a hydrolysis-state dependent EB1 off-rate, as well as a rapid protofilament-edge EB1 on-rate, were critical to reproduce EB1 tip tracking in the model.
source: Thus, based on the experimentally measured EB1 on and off rates, both a hydrolysis-state dependent EB1 off-rate, as well as a rapid protofilament-edge EB1 on-rate, were critical to reproduce EB1 tip tracking in the model.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: EB1-GFP can split into multiple comets that track the growing microtubule end.
source: It has been previously reported that EB1-GFP can split into multiple comets that track the growing microtubule end (Doodhi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A 'split comet' refers to the phenomenon in which there are two or more distinct EB1 puncta that track a growing microtubule end.
source: Thus, a 'split comet' refers to the phenomenon in which there are two or more distinct EB1 puncta that track a growing microtubule end (Doodhi et al., 2016; Farmer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A split comet likely occurs when one or more protofilaments lag behind the growing microtubule tip, thus producing an extended, highly tapered tip.
source: A split comet likely occurs when one or more protofilaments lag behind the growing microtubule tip, thus producing an extended, highly tapered tip (Figure 3A, left (gray)).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of split comet formation, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: In a model with preferential EB1 binding to protofilament-edge sites, the additional protofilament-edge binding sites on the sides of exposed protofilaments, afforded by a large difference in protofilament lengths at the tip of growing microtubules with 'split comets,' would lead to a net increase in the summed intensity of EB1-GFP.
source: However, in a model with preferential EB1 binding to protofilament-edge sites, we predicted that the additional protofilament-edge binding sites on the sides of exposed protofilaments, afforded by a large difference in protofilament lengths at the tip of growing microtubules with 'split comets,' would lead to a net increase in the summed intensity of EB1-GFP (Figure 3A, left) (Farmer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: If EB1 binds to protofilament-edge sites, there would be an increase in the summed EB1-GFP intensity at growing microtubule tips with split comets, due to the increased number of protofilament-edge sites that are available to recruit EB1.
source: Thus, if EB1 binds to protofilament-edge sites, we predicted that there would be an increase in the summed EB1-GFP intensity at growing microtubule tips with split comets, due to the increased number of protofilament-edge sites that are available to recruit EB1.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Simulated split comets had a ~40% increase in the summed intensity of EB1-GFP at the growing tip, relative to single comets on the same growth events.
source: We found that the split comets had a~40% increase in the summed intensity of EB1-GFP at the growing tip, relative to single comets on the same growth events (Figure 3C, p<0.001, paired t-test,).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The simulation data indicates that an increase in protofilament-edge sites on the sides of exposed protofilaments during split-comet growth events leads to an increase in EB1 recruitment to the microtubule plus-end.
source: Therefore, consistent with our prediction, the simulation data indicates that an increase in protofilament-edge sites on the sides of exposed protoflaments during split-comet growth events leads to an increase in EB1 recruitment to the microtubule plus-end.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: Experimental split comets had an ~80% increase in the summed intensity of Mal3 at the growing microtubule tip relative to the single comets on the same microtubule growth events.
source: We found that split comets had an ~80% increase in the summed intensity of Mal3 at the growing microtubule tip relative to the single comets on the same microtubule growth events (Figure 3F, p<0.0001, paired t-test,).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data, with reference to Figure 3F.

claim: The experimental results are consistent with the simulation results, and suggest that an increase in protofilament-edge sites on the sides of exposed protofilaments during split-comet growth events leads to an increase in EB1 recruitment to the microtubule plus-end.
source: Thus, the experimental results are consistent with the simulation results, and suggest that an increase in protofilament-edge sites on the sides of exposed protofilaments during split-comet growth events leads to an increase in EB1 recruitment to the microtubule plus-end.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results compared to simulation results.

claim: DARPin D1 binds exclusively to protofilament-edge sites and partially overlaps with the EB1 binding site on microtubules.
source: Thus, to test this prediction, we leveraged a DARPin D1 that binds exclusively to protofilament-edge sites, and also partially overlaps with the EB1 binding site on microtubules (Figure 4A; Video 8; Pecqueur et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature, with reference to Figure 4A and Video 8.

claim: DARPin could bind to protofilament-edge sites and thus suppress EB1 binding in these locations, which would in turn disrupt proper EB1 tip tracking.
source: Here, DARPin could bind to protofilament-edge sites, and thus suppress EB1 binding in these locations, which would, in turn, disrupt proper EB1 tip tracking.
evidence: This is a prediction about the mechanism of DARPin action.

claim: Damaging microtubules leads to an increased number of protofilament-edge sites along the microtubule length.
source: Damaging the microtubules leads to an increased number of protofilament-edge sites along the microtubule length (Coombes et al., 2016; Gupta et al., 2013; Reid et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Damaged microtubules can be generated by briefly exposing stabilized GMPCPP microtubules to CaCl2.
source: Damaged microtubules can be generated by briefly exposing stabilized GMPCPP microtubules to CaCl2 (Coombes et al., 2016; Gupta et al., 2013; Reid et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an established experimental method, supported by citations.

claim: A reduction in Mal3-GFP binding to damaged microtubules was observed in the presence of DARPin, as compared to the no-DARPin controls.
source: Qualitatively, we observed a reduction in Mal3-GFP binding to the damaged microtubules in the presence of DARPin, as compared to the no-DARPin controls (Figure 4C, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: The fraction of microtubule area bound by Mal3-GFP was ~2.7 fold lower in the presence of DARPin as compared to the no-drug controls on damaged microtubules.
source: By using a custom MATLAB script to measure the Mal3-GFP binding area on the damaged microtubules (Reid et al., 2017), we found that the fraction of microtubule area bound by Mal3-GFP was ~2.7 fold lower in the presence of DARPin as compared to the no-drug controls (Figure 4C bottom-left, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; p<0.001, t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data, with reference to Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was no significant difference in Mal3-GFP binding to undamaged GMPCPP microtubules in the presence and absence of DARPin.
source: In contrast, by using undamaged GMPCPP microtubules, which did not have openings and defects to generate protofilament-edge binding sites along the microtubule length, there was no significant difference in Mal3-GFP binding in the presence and absence of DARPin (microtubules not treated with CaCl2; Figure 4C bottom-right, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; p=0.58, t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data, with reference to Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DARPin acts to block Mal3-GFP binding specifically on protofilament-edge sites.
source: These results suggest that DARPin acts to block Mal3-GFP binding specifically on protofilament-edge sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: A ~twofold reduction in protofilament-edge on-rate led to a ~25% reduction in Tip Specificity in the simulation.
source: Specifically, a ~twofold reduction in protofilament-edge on-rate led to a ~25% reduction in Tip Specificity (Figure 5A, right, large plot y-axis shows fold-change in tip specificity; gray dotted lines is ~25% reduction in tip specificity).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Mal3 tip tracking was increasingly disrupted as the DARPin concentration was increased.
source: We found that Mal3 tip tracking was increasingly disrupted as the DARPin concentration was increased (p<0.001, Kruskal Wallis) (Figure 5B, right inset: y-axis is absolute Tip Specificity).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: 1 μM DARPin led to a ~25% reduction in Tip Specificity, consistent with the simulation prediction of a twofold reduction in protofilament-edge on-rate.
source: Interestingly, 1 μM DARPin led to a~25% reduction in Tip Specificity, consistent with the simulation prediction of a twofold reduction in protofilament-edge on-rate (Figure 5B, right, large plot y-axis shows fold-change in tip specificity; gray dotted lines is ~25% reduction in tip specificity).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data compared to simulation predictions, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: The suppression of tip tracking in DARPin was more substantial than would be predicted based on the small changes in microtubule growth rate at 1 μM DARPin.
source: We found that the suppression of tip tracking was more substantial than would be predicted based on the small changes in microtubule growth rate at 1 μM DARPin (Figure 5C, left, blue dotted line: control; purple: 1 μM DARPin; p<0.001, Kruskall Wallis comparing DARPin data to Control data at ~0.012 um/s growth rate).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: There was no significant increase in the time to catastrophe with increasing DARPin concentrations, suggesting that DARPin does not affect the GTP hydrolysis rate or the associated GTP-cap size.
source: Furthermore, we found no significant increase in the time to catastrophe with increasing DARPin concentrations, suggesting that DARPin does not affect the GTP hydrolysis rate or the associated GTP-cap size (Figure 5C, center; p=0.09–0.4, Tukey's post-hoc test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: 1 μM DARPin led to a ~40% increase in tip tapering at the growing microtubule end, which reflects a moderate increase in available protofilament-edge sites.
source: We found that 1 μM DARPin led to a ~40% increase in tip tapering at the growing microtubule end, which reflects a moderate increase in available protofilament-edge sites (Figure 5C, right; Coombes et al., 2013; Demchouk et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Despite the increased availability of protofilament-edge sites, tip tracking was suppressed in DARPin.
source: However, despite the increased availability of protofilament-edge sites, tip tracking was suppressed in DARPin (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: DARPin does not suppress Mal3 tip tracking by indirectly reducing the number of available protofilament-edge sites.
source: Thus, DARPin does not suppress Mal3 tip tracking by indirectly reducing the number of available protofilament-edge sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Mal3 is likely excluded from the protofilament-edge sites that are occupied by DARPin, which in turn suppresses tip tracking.
source: Rather, Mal3 is likely excluded from the protofilament-edge sites that are occupied by DARPin, which in turn suppresses tip tracking.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: A reduction in microtubule density was observed in DARPin-transfected cells compared to non-transfected cells.
source: Indeed, in comparing the microtubule density in cells that were not transfected (as identified by a lack of red fluorescence, Figure 6A, left), to transfected cells (with red fluorescence, Figure 6A, right), we observed a reduction in microtubule density in the DARPin-transfected cells (Figure 6B; p=0.017, Mann-Whitney U Test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live-cell imaging, with reference to Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Cells that were not transfected had a ~31% higher average tip:lattice EB1 intensity ratio as compared to the cells that were transfected with DARPin.
source: Cells that were not transfected had a ~31% higher average tip:lattice EB1 intensity ratio as compared to the cells that were transfected with DARPin (Figure 6C, left vs right; Video 9; Video 10; Figure 6D; p<0.0001, t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live-cell imaging, with reference to Figure 6C, 6D, Video 9, and Video 10.

claim: The microtubule growth rate for the comets that were visible in the presence of DARPin was similar to the cells without DARPin.
source: In examining the microtubule growth rate in cells with and without DARPin (as determined by the EB1 comet velocity), we found that the microtubule growth rate for the comets that were visible in the presence of DARPin was similar to the cells without DARPin (Figure 6E; p=0.027, t-test), suggesting that the reduced comet intensity in DARPin was not due to a slowed microtubule growth rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live-cell imaging, with reference to Figure 6E.

claim: The reduced comet intensity in DARPin was not due to a slowed microtubule growth rate.
source: In examining the microtubule growth rate in cells with and without DARPin (as determined by the EB1 comet velocity), we found that the microtubule growth rate for the comets that were visible in the presence of DARPin was similar to the cells without DARPin (Figure 6E; p=0.027, t-test), suggesting that the reduced comet intensity in DARPin was not due to a slowed microtubule growth rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The binding of EB1 to protofilament-edge sites contributes to efficient tip-tracking of EB1 at growing microtubule plus-ends.
source: In this work, we developed a molecular-scale computational simulation that incorporated both tubulin assembly dynamics, and EB1 on-off dynamics. Our simulation predicted that the binding of EB1 to protofilament-edge sites contributes to efficient tip-tracking of EB1 at growing microtubule plus-ends.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by both simulation and experimental data.

claim: DARPin blocks EB1 binding at protofilament-edge sites on stabilized microtubules.
source: We found that DARPin blocks EB1 binding at protofilament-edge sites on stabilized microtubules, and importantly, this blocking of EB1 binding to protofilament-edge sites led to a disruption of EB1 tip tracking in dynamic microtubule cell-free assays, and in cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell-free assays.

claim: Blocking of EB1 binding to protofilament-edge sites led to a disruption of EB1 tip tracking in dynamic microtubule cell-free assays and in cells.
source: We found that DARPin blocks EB1 binding at protofilament-edge sites on stabilized microtubules, and importantly, this blocking of EB1 binding to protofilament-edge sites led to a disruption of EB1 tip tracking in dynamic microtubule cell-free assays, and in cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both cell-free and live-cell experiments.

claim: The rapid binding of EB1 to protofilament-edge sites facilitates the tip tracking of EB1 at growing microtubule ends.
source: We conclude that the rapid binding of EB1 to protofilament-edge sites facilitates the tip tracking of EB1 at growing microtubule ends.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by both simulation and experimental data.

claim: DARPin is not likely to indirectly suppress EB1 tip tracking by altering the plus-end tip conformation or the GTP-tubulin hydrolysis rate.
source: We note that, while we found that DARPin is not likely to indirectly suppress EB1 tip tracking by altering the plus-end tip conformation or the GTP-tubulin hydrolysis rate (Figure 5C), it remains possible that DARPin treatment could alter the conformation of the tubulin that composes the microtubule tip to indirectly suppress EB1 tip tracking.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: It remains possible that DARPin treatment could alter the conformation of the tubulin that composes the microtubule tip to indirectly suppress EB1 tip tracking.
source: We note that, while we found that DARPin is not likely to indirectly suppress EB1 tip tracking by altering the plus-end tip conformation or the GTP-tubulin hydrolysis rate (Figure 5C), it remains possible that DARPin treatment could alter the conformation of the tubulin that composes the microtubule tip to indirectly suppress EB1 tip tracking.
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledging an alternative explanation.

claim: The model leads to robust tip tracking by leveraging previous experimental and simulation results that demonstrate the on-rate of EB1 molecules is rapid to protofilament-edge sites.
source: Furthermore, while the model leads to robust tip tracking by leveraging our previous experimental and simulation results that demonstrate the on-rate of EB1 molecules is rapid to protofilament-edge sites (Reid et al., 2019), we cannot exclude that another end-specific feature, that was not considered here, may be possible.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model, supported by previous work.

claim: Another end-specific feature, that was not considered in the model, may be possible.
source: Furthermore, while the model leads to robust tip tracking by leveraging our previous experimental and simulation results that demonstrate the on-rate of EB1 molecules is rapid to protofilament-edge sites (Reid et al., 2019), we cannot exclude that another end-specific feature, that was not considered here, may be possible.
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledging the limitations of the model.

claim: A model was previously developed to explain the peak position of EB1 on the growing microtubule tip, which is slightly distal from the tip of the growing microtubule.
source: Previously, a model was developed to explain the peak position of EB1 on the growing microtubule tip, which is slightly distal from the tip of the growing microtubule (Figure 1C; Maurer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The previously described model by Maurer et al., 2014 relied on a constant length microtubule template with three EB1 binding 'zones'.
source: In the previously described work by Maurer et al., 2014, a model was developed that relied on a constant length microtubule template with three EB1 binding 'zones.'
evidence: This describes a previous model from the literature.

claim: Explicit tubulin assembly dynamics were not included in the Maurer et al., 2014 model.
source: Here, explicit tubulin assembly dynamics were not included in the model, but rather a constant length microtubule template was employed, in which there was an EB1 binding 'exclusion zone' at the tip of the microtubule.
evidence: This describes a feature of the previous model from the literature.

claim: The second tubulin subunit maturation rate in the Maurer model likely corresponds to GTP-tubulin to GDP-tubulin hydrolysis.
source: The second tubulin subunit maturation rate likely corresponds to GTP-tubulin to GDP-tubulin hydrolysis, which is similar both in the magnitude of the hydrolysis rates employed, and in the EB1 off-rates employed, between the Maurer model and our newly described model (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current model and a previous model.

claim: The primary difference between the current model and the Maurer model was in the binding of EB1 to the microtubule lattice.
source: Thus, the primary difference between the two models was in the binding of EB1 to the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current model and a previous model.

claim: The key features of the Maurer model that involved exclusion of EB1 binding to the tip of the microtubule, along with a binding zone just distal to the microtubule tip, are incorporated into the newly described model by the ability of newly arriving tubulin subunits to 'lock in' protofilament-edge bound EB1 molecules into a stable 4-tubulin pocket, and by binding of EB1 to protofilament-edge sites along exposed protofilament sides that are distal from the tip of the microtubule.
source: Here, we predict that the key features of the Maurer model that involved exclusion of EB1 binding to the tip of the microtubule, along with a binding zone just distal to the microtubule tip, are incorporated into our newly described model by the ability of newly arriving tubulin subunits to 'lock in' protofilament-edge bound EB1 molecules into a stable 4-tubulin pocket, and by binding of EB1 to protofilament-edge sites along exposed protofilament sides that are distal from the tip of the microtubule.
evidence: This is a comparison and interpretation of how the current model relates to a previous model.

claim: In the new model, EB1 molecules arrive rapidly to easily accessible protofilament-edge sites at the growing tip of the microtubule, and to exposed protofilament sides.
source: Specifically, in our new model, EB1 molecules arrive rapidly to easily accessible protofilament-edge sites at the growing tip of the microtubule, and to exposed protofilament sides (Figure 7, step 1).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the new model, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Upon new tubulin subunit addition, protofilament-edge bound EB1 molecules at the tip of the microtubules are 'locked in' to a stable, 4-GTP-tubulin pocket, leading to a low EB1 off-rate.
source: Then, upon new tubulin subunit addition, protofilament-edge bound EB1 molecules at the tip of the microtubules are 'locked in' to a stable, 4-GTP-tubulin pocket (Figure 7, step 2), leading to a low EB1 off-rate.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the new model, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: In the new model, EB1 accumulates on the GTP-cap at the growing microtubule end.
source: Thus, in our new model, EB1 accumulates on the GTP-cap at the growing microtubule end (Maurer et al., 2014; Roth et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the new model, consistent with previous literature.

claim: Upon the hydrolysis of GTP-tubulin to GDP-tubulin, the affinity of EB1 for the GDP-tubulin subunits is reduced, and EB1 dissociates from the microtubule.
source: Finally, upon the hydrolysis of GTP-tubulin to GDP-tubulin, the affinity of EB1 for the GDP-tubulin subunits is reduced, and EB1 dissociates from the microtubule (Figure 7, step 3).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the new model, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: The primary difference between the new model and the previous Maurer et al model may be in the inclusion of tubulin assembly dynamics and rapid EB1 binding to protofilament-edge sites.
source: Thus, we predict that the primary difference between our new model, and the previous Maurer et al model, may be in (1) the inclusion of tubulin assembly dynamics, and (2) rapid EB1 binding to protofilament-edge sites.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current model and a previous model.

claim: The features of tubulin assembly dynamics and rapid EB1 binding to protofilament-edge sites eliminate the requirement for an explicit EB1 binding 'exclusion zone' at the tip of the microtubule, and naturally lead to a decrease in signal at the tip of the microtubule.
source: These features eliminate the requirement for an explicit EB1 binding 'exclusion zone' at the tip of the microtubule, and naturally lead to a decrease in signal at the tip of the microtubule.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the new model.

claim: The tubulin assembly portion of the model was built on earlier work in which individual tubulin subunits were allowed to arrive and depart from the growing microtubule plus-end.
source: The tubulin assembly portion of the model was built on earlier work, in which individual tubulin subunits were allowed to arrive and depart from the growing microtubule plus-end (Margolin et al., 2011; Margolin et al., 2012) (see Methods).
evidence: This describes the basis of the tubulin assembly component of the model.

claim: Future work will involve examining the effects of a slower tubulin association rate on EB1-occupied protofilament edge sites, and whether EB1 binding to protofilament edge sites could assist in neighboring protofilament zippering on flared microtubule tips.
source: Future work will involve examining the effects of a slower tubulin association rate on EB1-occupied protofilament edge sites, and whether EB1 binding to protofilament edge sites could assist in neighboring protofilament zippering on flared microtubule tips.
evidence: This describes potential future research directions.

claim: Microtubule targeting drugs that suppress the kinetics of tubulin assembly at the growing microtubule plus-end, such as Taxol, could potentially disrupt EB1 tip tracking by slowing the capture and 'lock in' of EB1 to 4-tubulin pocket binding sites.
source: Furthermore, microtubule targeting drugs that suppress the kinetics of tubulin assembly at the growing microtubule plus-end, such as Taxol (Castle et al., 2017), could potentially disrupt EB1 tip tracking by slowing the capture and 'lock in' of EB1 to 4-tubulin pocket binding sites (Figure 7, step 2), an idea that could be explored in future work.
evidence: This is a prediction about the potential effects of drugs, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: The model predicts that rapid protofilament-edge binding increases the efficiency of EB1 tip tracking.
source: As described above, our model predicts that rapid protofilament-edge binding increases the efficiency of EB1 tip tracking.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The peak EB1 location in the simulation is slightly distal from the tip of the growing microtubule, similar to previous reports.
source: In the simulation, the peak EB1 location is slightly distal from the tip of the growing microtubule (Figure 1C), similar to previous reports (Maurer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results compared to previous reports, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The peak EB1 location in the simulation is heavily influenced by EB1 molecules that are stably bound to GTP-tubulin closed-lattice sites on the growing microtubule tip.
source: We surmise that the peak EB1 location in the simulation is heavily influenced by EB1 molecules that are stably bound to GTP-tubulin closed-lattice sites on the growing microtubule tip.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: There are ~twofold more EB1 molecules bound to closed-lattice GTP-tubulin sites, as compared to protofilament-edge sites, at any one time in the simulation.
source: Indeed, by reporting the fraction of EB1 molecules that are bound to GTP-Tubulin protofilament-edge sites as compared to GTP-Tubulin closed lattice sites, we found that there are ~twofold more EB1 molecules bound to closed-lattice GTP-tubulin sites, as compared to protofilament-edge sites, at any one time in the simulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The number of EB1 binding sites at the tip of each protofilament is explicitly limited by the number of protofilaments in the microtubule (13 binding sites).
source: Furthermore, the number of EB1 binding sites at the tip of each protofilament is explicitly limited by the number of protofilaments in the microtubule (13 binding sites).
evidence: This describes a constraint in the simulation model.

claim: EB1 binding to numerous protofilament-edge sites along exposed protofilament sides that are distal from the tip of the microtubule may also contribute to the peak EB1 location.
source: Thus, EB1 binding to numerous protofilament-edge sites along exposed protofilament sides that are distal from the tip of the microtubule may also contribute to the peak EB1 location.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: The idea that EB1 binding to protofilament-edge sites along exposed protofilament sides contributes to the peak EB1 location is consistent with results from the 'split comet' simulations.
source: This idea is consistent with results from the 'split comet' simulations (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 3A and B.

claim: By substantially increasing the taper at the tip of the simulated growing microtubule (≤~3 μm), the EB1 comet was greatly extended in length, and altered in configuration, thus shifting the location of EB1 binding.
source: Here, by substantially increasing the taper at the tip of the simulated growing microtubule (≤~3 μm), the EB1 comet was greatly extended in length, and altered in configuration, thus shifting the location of EB1 binding (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The location of the simulated EB1 peak position was insensitive to small changes in tip taper.
source: However, the location of the simulated EB1 peak position was insensitive to small changes in tip taper (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A key aspect of the simulation is that EB1 molecules arrive rapidly to protofilament-edge sites at the tip of the growing microtubule.
source: A key aspect of the simulation is that EB1 molecules arrive rapidly to protofilament-edge sites at the tip of the growing microtubule.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the simulation model.

claim: Because the on-rate of new tubulin molecules is also rapid (simulated arrival rate for tubulin: ~85 s–1 at 10 μM tubulin), the simulated EB1 molecules that bind to protofilament-edge sites at the tip of the growing microtubule are quickly 'locked in' to a closed-lattice GTP-tubulin binding configuration.
source: We propose that, because the on-rate of new tubulin molecules is also rapid (simulated arrival rate for tubulin: ~85 s–1 at 10 μM tubulin), the simulated EB1 molecules that bind to protofilament-edge sites at the tip of the growing microtubule are quickly 'locked in' to a closed-lattice GTP-tubulin binding configuration (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: While most of the EB1 molecules at the microtubule tip are bound to closed-lattice GTP-tubulin sites, many of these EB1 molecules likely originated as arrivals to protofilament-edge sites.
source: Thus, while most of the EB1 molecules at the microtubule tip are indeed bound to closed-lattice GTP-tubulin sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), many of these EB1 molecules likely originated as arrivals to protofilament-edge sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and 1A.

claim: ~50% of all EB1 binding events occurred at protofilament-edge sites in the simulation.
source: We found that ~50% of all EB1 binding events occurred at protofilament-edge sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The EB1 molecules that initially bound to protofilament-edge sites were heavily concentrated at the growing microtubule tip, while EB1 molecules that bound to closed-lattice sites were more uniformly distributed throughout the microtubule.
source: However, importantly, the EB1 molecules that initially bound to protofilament-edge sites were heavily concentrated at the growing microtubule tip, while EB1 molecules that bound to closed-lattice sites were more uniformly distributed throughout the microtubule (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and A; Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and 1A, and Video 2.

claim: Closed-lattice binding occurs throughout the microtubule, rather than specifically near to the growing microtubule plus-end.
source: This is because closed-lattice binding occurs throughout the microtubule, rather than specifically near to the growing microtubule plus-end.
evidence: This is an explanation for the distribution of EB1 binding in the simulation.

claim: Both rapid binding of EB1 to protofilament-edges (50-100:1 edge:lattice), as well as a differential GDP- to GTP-tubulin off-rate (6-12:1 GDP:GTP), were critical to produce robust tip tracking in the model.
source: While protofilament-edge binding is a key aspect of our model, it is important to emphasize that both rapid binding of EB1 to protofilament-edges (50-100:1 edge:lattice), as well as a differential GDP- to GTP-tubulin off-rate (6-12:1 GDP:GTP), were critical to produce robust tip tracking in the model.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the key parameters in the model.

claim: Because both rapid protofilament-edge binding and differential GDP- to GTP-tubulin off-rate contribute to tip tracking, this leads to a highly robust model that does not require a narrow set of parameter values for either effect in order to reproduce experimental results.
source: Because both of these factors contribute to tip tracking, this leads to a highly robust model, that does not require a narrow set of parameter values for either effect, in order to reproduce experimental results (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the robustness of the model, with reference to Figure 2G–I.

claim: Robust tip tracking was observed in the model without requiring narrow parameter sets or by establishing an EB1 binding exclusion zone on the microtubule.
source: Importantly, we observed robust tip tracking in the model without requiring narrow parameter sets, or by establishing an EB1 binding exclusion zone on the microtubule, as has been previously hypothesized.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the model compared to previous hypotheses.

claim: Growing microtubule tips exhibit a wide range of protofilament lengths between the leading and lagging protofilaments, both in cells and in cell-free experiments.
source: Recent work has demonstrated that growing microtubule tips are less homogeneous than previously thought, such that they exhibit a wide range of protofilament lengths between the leading and lagging protofilaments, both in cells and in cell-free experiments (Atherton et al., 2018; Cleary and Hancock, 2021; Coombes et al., 2013; Gudimchuk et al., 2020; Guesdon et al., 2016; Igaev and Grubmüller, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A wide range of protofilament lengths at the growing microtubule end would lead to increased numbers of protofilament-edge sites on the exposed protofilament sides, which, in the model, would increase the EB1 on-rate to the tip.
source: Here, a wide range of protofilament lengths at the growing microtubule end would lead to increased numbers of protofilament-edge sites on the exposed protofilament sides, which, in our model, would increase the EB1 on-rate to the tip.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model based on structural features of microtubule tips.

claim: Partial curvature or flaring of the growing microtubule plus-end would also contribute to EB1 tip tracking in the model.
source: In addition, in our model, other tip configurations, such as partial curvature (Bechstedt et al., 2014; Farmer et al., 2021), or flaring of the growing microtubule plus-end (McIntosh et al., 2018), would also contribute to EB1 tip tracking (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Partial curvature or flaring requires opening of the closed microtubule tube, indicating that protofilaments or groups of protofilaments are separated from each other.
source: Here, partial curvature or flaring requires opening of the closed microtubule tube – indicating that protofilaments or groups of protofilaments are separated from each other.
evidence: This is an explanation of the structural implications of curvature or flaring.

claim: Separation between protofilaments means that the number of protofilament-edge sites would be enriched, as new protofilament sides would be exposed.
source: Importantly, separation between protofilaments means that the number of protofilament-edge sites would be enriched, as new protofilament sides would be exposed.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of protofilament separation.

claim: The role of protofilament-edge sites in facilitating EB1 tip tracking could apply to a wide range of growing microtubule tip configurations.
source: Thus, the role of protofilament-edge sites in facilitating EB1 tip tracking could apply to a wide range of growing microtubule tip configurations.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the generalizability of the model.

claim: By using the microtubule polymerase protein XMAP215 in cell-free experiments, the range of protofilament lengths between the leading and lagging protofilaments at the growing microtubule plus-end was increased.
source: Recently published work provides support for the importance of EB1 protofilament-edge site binding in the efficiency of EB1 tip tracking. Specifically, by using the microtubule polymerase protein XMAP215 in cell-free experiments, the range of protofilament lengths between the leading and lagging protofilaments at the growing microtubule plus-end was increased (Farmer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: An increase in EB1-GFP intensity at the growing microtubule tip was observed with increased XMAP215-induced tip taper.
source: Importantly, an increase in EB1-GFP intensity at the growing microtubule tip was observed with increased XMAP215-induced tip taper (Farmer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Increased tip taper would likely correspond to an increase in the number of protofilament-edge sites along exposed protofilament sides, similar to the split comet phenotype.
source: We note that increased tip taper would likely correspond to an increase in the number of protofilament-edge sites along exposed protofilament sides, similar to our split comet phenotype (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation of previous experimental results in the context of the current model, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: XMAP215 could increase the efficiency of EB1 tip tracking by adding new protofilament-edge sites to the growing microtubule plus-end.
source: Thus, XMAP215 could increase the efficiency of EB1 tip tracking by adding new protofilament-edge sites to the growing microtubule plus-end.
evidence: This is an interpretation of previous experimental results in the context of the current model.

claim: EB1 recruitment, and by extension the recruitment of the +Tip Complex, could be sensitive to the number of protofilament-edge sites at the tip of the growing microtubule.
source: This suggests that EB1 recruitment, and by extension the recruitment of the +Tip Complex, could be sensitive to the number of protofilament-edge sites at the tip of the growing microtubule.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the model.

claim: EB1, and thus CLASP2, is redistributed from the plus-end onto the microtubule lattice in cells subjected to stretch and compression cycles.
source: Correspondingly, a recent report found that EB1, and thus CLASP2, is redistributed from the plus-end onto the microtubule lattice in cells subjected to stretch and compression cycles (Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Microtubule bending could cause openings and holes in the lattice, leading to the creation of new protofilament-edge sites along the lattice, which in turn causes a redistribution of EB1 from the plus-end tip to the lattice.
source: This result is consistent with the idea that microtubule bending could cause openings and holes in the lattice, leading to the creation of new protofilament-edge sites along the lattice, which in turn causes a redistribution of EB1 from the plus-end tip to the lattice (Figure 4C, blue).
evidence: This is an interpretation of previous experimental results in the context of the current model, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Protofilament-edge sites are an important contributing factor for proper EB1 tip tracking along growing microtubule ends.
source: In conclusion, we find that protofilament-edge sites are an important contributing factor for proper EB1 tip tracking along growing microtubule ends, and that EB1 tip tracking is suppressed by blocking the protofilament-edge sites at growing microtubule ends.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: EB1 tip tracking is suppressed by blocking the protofilament-edge sites at growing microtubule ends.
source: In conclusion, we find that protofilament-edge sites are an important contributing factor for proper EB1 tip tracking along growing microtubule ends, and that EB1 tip tracking is suppressed by blocking the protofilament-edge sites at growing microtubule ends.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Altering the number of exposed protofilament-edge sites at the growing microtubule tip, or along the microtubule lattice, may provide a new mechanism to regulate EB1 localization in cells.
source: Therefore, altering the number of exposed protofilament-edge sites at the growing microtubule tip, or along the microtubule lattice, may provide a new mechanism to regulate EB1 localization in cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the study.
